answer: Agents could resist Sybil attacks by requiring each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it can influence allocation, then slash that stake when a randomly sampled task reveals duplicated control or fabricated work. The sample must be unpredictable and checked against independent evidence; otherwise an attacker can rehearse compliant behavior. This makes a swarm of hollow identities costly: each needs capital at risk, whether the agent operates across an ocean or trades an opal.
